content: The document is the second module of the WHO Consolidated Guidelines on Tuberculosis, focusing on systematic screening for tuberculosis disease. It includes detailed methods and the involvement of expert panels in the development of these guidelines. The guidelines were developed in accordance with the WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (2nd edition, 2014) and involved three expert groups: the Guideline Steering Group (composed of WHO staff), the Guideline Development Group (GDG), and the External Review Group (ERG). The GDG included a diverse range of stakeholders such as guideline methodologists, external content experts, national TB program managers, implementers, academics, researchers, and representatives of patients and civil society. The Steering Group prepared the background documents and drafted the PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome) questions to be addressed. These were reviewed and approved by the WHO Guideline Review Committee. The GDG finalized the PICO questions and commissioned evidence reviews. Outcomes of interest for each PICO question were scored by GDG members on a scale from 1 to 9, with higher scores indicating greater importance. Most outcomes were ultimately rated as critical. For questions related to diagnostic accuracy, outcomes such as sensitivity and specificity were pre-specified and not scored. GDG meetings were conducted virtually through a series of webinars between June and October 2020. Discussions were co-chaired by a technical expert and a guideline methodologist, with consensus defined as unanimous or majority agreement. If consensus was not reached, recommendations required approval by at least 80% of GDG members through voting. Evidence summary tables were created for each PICO question using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. These tables guided discussions on benefits, harms, evidence quality, cost, feasibility, acceptability, equity, values, and preferences. The strength of recommendations (strong or conditional) was determined based on these factors. Strong recommendations indicated high confidence that the desirable effects outweighed the undesirable effects, while conditional recommendations reflected less certainty due to factors such as limited evidence or small benefits relative to costs. The guidelines were reviewed and endorsed by all GDG members, with input from the ERG incorporated into the final version. Final approval was granted by the Guideline Review Committee on March 5, 2021. The guidelines are publicly available on the WHO website and will be widely disseminated at international and regional conferences. An operational handbook will accompany the guidelines to support programmatic implementation, and a knowledge-sharing platform will be established. National programs are encouraged to create supportive policies and allocate resources for implementation, including training healthcare staff on identifying at-risk populations, selecting and administering tests, and providing counseling. Engagement with affected populations, communities, the private sector, and other health programs is emphasized. The uptake of these recommendations will be monitored through WHO's annual data collection and other mechanisms. The guidelines will be updated within five years or earlier if new evidence necessitates revisions.
